revisions.title: From display to definition
revisions.body: One way to hear this opening is as a test of whether a performance can survive a demand for a name. Socrates declines another display and asks for conversation about Gorgias’s art. When Polus praises the finest art instead of naming it, Socrates restores the question’s exact form.

revisions.title: Rhetoric tested against expertise
revisions.body: After separating belief from knowledge, Socrates gives rhetoric a narrow test: it produces belief rather than instruction about just and unjust. In choosing doctors, shipbuilders, architects, or generals, he says, the relevant experts—not rhetoricians—should advise. Gorgias answers with Themistocles and Pericles, claiming that their counsel produced Athenian public works. Read the turn as a live dispute over civic influence, not as a settled demonstration.

revisions.title: From rhetorical power to user responsibility
revisions.body: Gorgias shifts the issue from rhetoric’s reach to its responsibility: by comparing rhetoric with boxing, pankration, and armed training, he argues that neither the art nor its teacher is blameworthy when a practitioner uses the skill unjustly; blame belongs to the user. Socrates then marks this defense as potentially inconsistent with Gorgias’s earlier account, preparing the refutation.

revisions.title: From crowd to epistemic asymmetry
revisions.body: The audience's request keeps the exchange alive, but the argument turns when Socrates recasts Gorgias's qualification—persuasive “in a crowd”—as persuasive among those who do not know. Gorgias accepts the result: a non-knower can persuade non-knowers more effectively than a knower. Socrates then generalizes: rhetoric need not know the matters themselves; it needs a device that makes ignorance look like knowledge. The question becomes whether persuasion can substitute for expertise.

revisions.title: A conclusion built from assent
revisions.body: Gorgias says a student who lacks knowledge of justice will learn it from him [claim_gorgias_0040]. Socrates then extends the craft analogy: within this chain of assents, the learner becomes just, so the rhetorician appears unable to wish injustice [obs_gorgias_0445; obs_gorgias_0446; claim_gorgias_0043; claim_gorgias_0044]. He recalls the earlier rule that misuse indicts the user, not the teacher [obs_gorgias_0023; claim_gorgias_0045]. The collision is Socrates’ claimed result, not a settled proof; the record notes qualified assents [claim_gorgias_0046].

revisions.title: From craft to a shared pursuit
revisions.body: Polus now takes the questioner’s role. One way to hear Socrates’ reply is as a shift from a status label—craft—to a description of what a practice produces. In Socrates’ stated view, rhetoric is no technē but an empeiria aimed at gratification and pleasure; he gives opso-poetic the same formula, while leaving their common pursuit unnamed.

revisions.title: The interlocutor as witness
revisions.body: Socrates redraws the rules of refutation. Polus may summon a crowd of reputable Athenians, but Socrates says that numbers do not establish truth; the decisive witness is the interlocutor who must agree. He explicitly sets this against another “mode of refutation” attributed to Polus and many others. One way to hear the turn is as a move from public assent to accountable dialogue.

revisions.title: From shameful to worse
revisions.body: Polus’s resistance exposes the hinge of the argument: he accepts that doing injustice is more shameful but refuses to call it worse. Socrates therefore makes “more shameful” comparative rather than merely rhetorical: it must exceed the other act in pain, badness, or both. Once Polus denies greater pain, the argument leaves badness as the remaining ground—and the rejected conclusion returns as his own assent.

revisions.title: A chain of assent, not a settled proof
revisions.body: Socrates’s main move here is a chain of assent, not a completed proof. He leads Polus from the claim that punishment is just through the claims that just things are fine and fine things good, ending in the proposal that the punished person may be benefited and become better in soul. The qualification matters: Socrates presents that improvement as his own supposition, while Polus calls it likely. Hear the hierarchy as an argument still being advanced, not as a settled conclusion.

revisions.title: Rhetoric under pressure
revisions.body: On the agreements now in force, Socrates pictures wrongdoing as a disease and punishment as a doctor's treatment; rhetoric would serve by exposing the wrong, not defending it. Then he reverses the case: if one wants an enemy harmed, rhetoric seems useful for helping a wrongdoer escape trial, repayment, or death. I hear this as a conditional pressure test, not a flat definition. Polus calls the result strange, yet admits it may follow from what came before.

revisions.title: The hinge: which standard judges justice
revisions.body: The move to hear here is Callicles’ change of standard. He says the verdict depends on whether the judge is convention or nature: convention condemns doing injustice, while nature makes suffering it worse and more shameful. He then charges Socrates with switching registers in mid-question. Whether or not that charge succeeds, it gives the dispute a precise fault line: which standard can judge justice?

revisions.title: Callicles' practical test for philosophy
revisions.body: Callicles makes age the boundary between education and failure: philosophy may train a youth, but in an older man it becomes ridiculous, even unmanly. He then turns that verdict into a practical courtroom test—what could a philosopher say under accusation?—and ends by urging Socrates toward practical affairs, reputation, and goods. This is Callicles’ standard, asserted here rather than tested.

revisions.title: Keep the figures distinct
revisions.body: Callicles reverses the ranking: temperance is foolish, while the right life enlarges desire and supplies it; needing nothing would make stones and corpses happiest. Socrates reports a myth from an unnamed wise man. Keep its figures distinct: the desire-bearing part is the leaky jar; the foolish soul appears as a leaky sieve. I read this as a test of Callicles’ definition of happiness, not as a new doctrine.

revisions.title: A pattern that separates pleasure from good
revisions.body: Socrates’ method here is to change the comparison. He offers health and disease as a pattern in which opposed conditions are gained and lost in turn, then extends that pattern toward goods and bads. When Callicles grants that thirst and pleasure cease together, Socrates contrasts that pair with the good and bad. The closing inference is Socrates’ argument; the accepted record does not establish that Callicles accepts it.

revisions.title: When pleasure becomes rhetoric's test
revisions.body: The hinge here is a change in the test. Socrates strips poetry down to its speeches, then classifies that speech by its audience and aim: rhetoric addressed to a mixed crowd becomes, in his account, flattery. He carries the same question toward civic oratory: should speech make citizens better, or merely gratify them? The arts are examples; the deeper issue is what counts as success for rhetoric.

revisions.title: Order as the orator's standard
revisions.body: Here Socrates turns the craft analogy into a standard for rhetoric: order gives the body health, while order in the soul is named justice and moderation. He then argues that restraining a disordered soul is better than leaving it licentious. Callicles says he does not know what Socrates means and does not care; Socrates therefore gives the unfinished argument a “head” and continues alone.

revisions.title: The hinge: order becomes a way of life
revisions.body: Socrates’ move is not just to praise temperance, but to make it the hinge of an ethical chain. Order first becomes the soul’s proper condition; the compact necessity sequence then turns temperance into fitting action toward humans and gods, justice, piety, courage, and finally happiness. One way to hear the argument’s force is that resisting one link would require reopening the whole chain.

revisions.title: Power That Protects—and Corrupts
revisions.body: Callicles accepts that escaping suffered injustice requires power; Socrates then extends the same demand to avoiding the doing of injustice, where power must be joined to craft. I read the turn that follows as a warning about moral direction: the power that secures safety can also make a person resemble an unjust ruler. Protection is therefore not self-justifying; its value depends on whether it prevents injustice or merely makes injustice safer to perform.

revisions.title: When survival is not yet a benefit
revisions.body: Socrates turns Callicles’ appeal to safety into a question about benefit. The pilot may bring passengers ashore alive, yet they leave no better than they arrived; Socrates then applies that distinction to a soul with incurable defects. The proposal is not that rescue has no value, but that survival by itself does not show that a life is better. He therefore asks us to consider living well, rather than merely living longer.

revisions.title: The test for public care
revisions.body: Socrates turns a moral distinction into a test of public competence: care aimed at pleasure is flattery, while genuine care aims to make its object better. The building analogy makes that test concrete—training and a record of worthwhile private work must precede public work—before Socrates applies the same standard to Callicles’ claim to improve citizens.

revisions.title: From hearsay to test
revisions.body: The hinge is Socrates’ shift from report to test. He presents Pericles’ alleged effect as hearsay, and Callicles rejects its source; the argument then proceeds conditionally from their prior standard that a good statesman makes citizens better. The herdsman analogy supplies that standard’s pressure, while Callicles’ qualified concession lets Socrates extend the same inference to Cimon, Themistocles, and Miltiades. Read this as an examination of political success, not a settled verdict.

revisions.title: Two models of civic care
revisions.body: Socrates turns the exchange into a forced choice about political service. He sets corrective care—like a doctor making Athenians better—against service aimed at gratifying them, then invokes Callicles’ own claim to frank speech and demands a clear answer. Callicles chooses service. The answer functions as a public self-positioning, not yet as a defended doctrine.

revisions.title: Political craft before a child jury
revisions.body: Socrates imagines his political work before a jury that rewards pleasure: like a doctor opposed by a pastry-cook before children, he would be shouted down even if he said he acted for health. Yet Socrates names a different, stronger kind of self-defence: having said or done nothing unjust toward people or gods. Death, he adds, is easier to bear than a soul burdened by injustice.

revisions.title: The soul before the judge
revisions.body: Here the myth turns character into a surface a judge can read. Socrates defines death, cautiously, as the separation of soul and body; then the soul, stripped of the body, displays what its practices have made of it. Within the myth’s qualified scheme, punishment benefits those with remediable offences, while the incurable become examples for others. The dramatic reversal is civic rank: Rhadamanthys is said to inspect a soul without knowing whose it is. The passage thus invites us to hear a king’s title as irrelevant to the verdict.
